name: Battle of Shanghai
info: China's National Revolutionary Army and Japan's Imperial Army fought for Shanghai from August to November 1937, in the Second Sino-Japanese War; Japan took the city at heavy cost to both sides and advanced on Nanjing.

facts.date: 13 August to 26 November 1937, in three stages: 13 to 22 August, 23 August to 26 October, and 27 October to the end of November
facts.place: Shanghai and its surroundings: the city's districts, the creek country to the north, the coast of the Yangtze delta and Hangzhou Bay, China
facts.sides: The Republic of China under Chiang Kai-shek, with commanders including Zhang Zhizhong and Chen Cheng; the Empire of Japan, with the Shanghai Expeditionary Army under Iwane Matsui. The battle eventually involved around one million troops. In early October the Japanese had more than 200,000 troops in the region against over 700,000 Chinese deployed across a wide front.
facts.outcome: The Japanese captured Shanghai after more than three months of fighting on land, in the air and at sea. China lost a significant portion of its best troops and no foreign power intervened.

t: Chinese estimates and Japanese claims of losses differ widely: China's official report of 5 November gave 187,200 killed and wounded, Japanese estimates were roughly 250,000, and the Japanese gave their own as 9,115 killed and 31,257 injured.

The Japanese expected to take Shanghai within days, but the Chinese held out for over three months, and Chiang Kai-shek lost much of his best-trained army, including some 10,000 of the 25,000 junior officers trained at Whampoa between 1929 and 1937.
Historian Peter Harmsen holds that the battle presaged urban combat as it was to be waged throughout the rest of the twentieth century; it was the largest urban battle before Stalingrad.
dyk: A Chinese air attack on the Japanese flagship Izumo on 14 August 1937 went wrong, and bombs fell on the Shanghai International Settlement; the day became known as Black Saturday.
ev: Two Japanese naval personnel and a Chinese guard are found dead at Hongqiao Airport, and the Japanese begin sending reinforcements to Shanghai
Fighting begins between Chinese and Japanese forces in Zhabei, Wusong and Jiangwan, and on 14 August China declares its resistance to Japanese aggression
The 36th Division's attack towards the Huangpu docks pushes the Japanese back but cannot break through
The Japanese 3rd and 11th Divisions land on the northeast coast, lengthening the front
Baoshan falls on 6 September, and the Chinese hold Luodian for weeks at heavy cost
The fight for Wusong Creek and Dachang ends with Dachang's fall on 26 October, and the Chinese withdraw from the city's urban centre
The Japanese 10th Army lands at Jinshanwei on 5 November, and on 8 November the Chinese order a general retreat
The Wufu Line is penetrated on 19 November and the Xicheng Line given up on 26 November, and the fighting runs on to Nanjing

sections.background:
Since the Japanese invasion of Manchuria in 1931 and the attack on Shanghai in 1932, China and Japan had been in armed conflict without an official declaration of war. These conflicts escalated in July 1937, when the Marco Polo Bridge Incident triggered a full-scale war. Shanghai was China's largest and most cosmopolitan city, the world's fifth largest at the time and the country's main commercial hub and largest port.

By deliberately starting a major conflict at Shanghai, the Chinese leadership is believed to have aimed to divert the main Japanese effort to the Yangtze delta, stalling their north-to-south advance, to give time to move vital industries to the interior, and to bring sympathetic Western powers to China's side. There is no consensus on whether the strategy succeeded.

On 9 August Naval Sub-Lieutenant Isao Ōyama and his driver were found dead at the gate of Hongqiao Airport together with a guard of the Chinese Peace Preservation Corps. On 10 August the Japanese Consul General demanded that the Chinese withdraw the Peace Preservation Corps and dismantle their defence works, and the Japanese began sending in reinforcements. Chinese troops were also deployed to the area from 11 August. Talks failed: Japan demanded a Chinese withdrawal from Shanghai, and Mayor Yu would concede at most that Chinese troops would not fire unless fired upon.
sections.forces:
The Chinese side was the National Revolutionary Army under Chiang Kai-shek. Zhang Zhizhong commanded the 5th Army and the Nanjing-Shanghai war zone at the start, and Chiang, with Chen Cheng and Gu Zhutong, later took over command duties. Its forces were equipped primarily with small-calibre weapons, against much greater Japanese air, naval and armour power, and the only heavy weapons it had against bunkers were 150 mm howitzers. The elite of its army were divisions trained and equipped by German advisers, among them Alexander von Falkenhausen.

The Japanese had the Special Naval Landing Forces in the city, bolstered by 1,400 marines on 18 August, and 6,300 by 19 August. On 15 August they formed the Shanghai Expeditionary Army from the 3rd and 11th Divisions under General Iwane Matsui, and later reinforced it with the 9th, 13th and 101st Divisions and other units. Their strongholds in the Hongkou salient were fortified with concrete, barbed wire, sandbags and machine guns, and the Third Fleet lay in the Huangpu.

Chiang's first plan was a surprise attack by the numerically superior Chinese to push the Japanese into the river, using Entscheidungsschlacht tactics recommended by Falkenhausen. Zhang estimated that it would take a week. By early October the Japanese had more than 200,000 troops in the region against over 700,000 Chinese, drawn from Chiang's own army and from units of many provincial and warlord armies.
sections.course:
Fighting began around 9 am on 13 August, when the Peace Preservation Corps exchanged fire with Japanese troops in Zhabei, Wusong and Jiangwan, and Japanese ships opened fire on Chinese positions. The Chinese offensive began on 14 August, but it was halted by the entrenched Japanese and by naval bombardment. A second assault, Iron Fist, began on 17 August and was called off by 18 August. The 36th Division then attacked towards the Huangpu docks from 19 August and by 21 August Chinese tanks reached Broadway, the last street before the river, but could not take the walled wharf.

On 23 August the Japanese 3rd and 11th Divisions landed on the northeast coast, some fifty kilometres from downtown Shanghai, and the front grew longer. The town of Baoshan fell on 6 September, and its defending battalion was killed apart from one soldier sent out with a message. The defence of Luodian, nicknamed the grinding mill of flesh and blood, cost the Chinese heavily, and by the end of September they gave it up. Fighting at Liujiahang and Gujiazhai followed.

In October the Japanese forced Wusong Creek and, after a Chinese counteroffensive failed on 21 October, took Dachang on 26 October. The Chinese left the city centre from that night, leaving a battalion to hold the Sihang Warehouse. The Japanese 10th Army landed at Jinshanwei on 5 November, and the Chinese ordered a general retreat on 8 November. The Wufu Line was penetrated on 19 November.
sections.aftermath:
China's official report of 5 November gave 187,200 killed and wounded. Contemporary Japanese estimates were roughly 250,000 Chinese casualties including some 67,000 killed, Frank Dorn put total Chinese casualties at 240,000 and Hsi-Sheng Chi at some 300,000. The Japanese claimed 9,115 killed and 31,257 injured, a figure Harmsen and Richard Frank think understated. Benjamin Lai estimates 93,000 to 99,000 Japanese casualties and James Paulose 92,640.

Chinese elite units suffered some sixty percent disproportionate casualties, and Chiang lost some 10,000 of the 25,000 junior officers trained at Whampoa between 1929 and 1937. By the time the 88th Division defended Nanjing it was down to seven thousand men, three thousand of them new recruits. Chiang had to rely more on provincial commanders of questionable loyalty, and lost some of his political leverage over local warlords. Almost all the Chinese tanks were lost.

Atrocities were committed, especially by the Japanese. According to Matsui's diary, all 500 Chinese prisoners captured around Wusong were shot, and Japanese forces machine-gunned crowds of refugees by the Jessfield Railway Bridge and strafed refugee columns. Aircraft struck ambulances marked with the Red Cross. The Chinese used scorched earth tactics, burning buildings and fields and poisoning wells. On Black Saturday, 14 August, errant Chinese bombs killed between 700 and 950 civilians outright, with some 3,000 civilian dead and injured, mostly at the Great World entertainment centre.
sections.sources:
The battle is known from official and unit records on both sides, from diaries and memoirs, and from eyewitnesses. Foreign journalists watched much of the fighting from the International Settlement; Edgar Snow compared it to Verdun on the Seine. Chinese records include the Ministry of Military Affairs' casualty counts and divisional reports, and Japanese ones include division statistics and battle summaries, Iwane Matsui's diary and the official records compiled by Ikuhiko Hata. Modern accounts rest on historians such as Peter Harmsen, Rana Mitter and Richard Frank.

The numbers are disputed. The Ministry of Military Affairs counted in 1938 some 229,382 Chinese casualties from 13 August to 15 November 1937, though Sichuan and Guangxi units had not reported, and put total losses at 300,000. A later ministry figure of 229,382 for the Third War Zone from the Marco Polo Bridge Incident to the fall of Nanjing matches it exactly. Chinese wartime records give over 60,000 Japanese casualties, Jonathan Fenby some 70,000. Units on both sides claimed each other's losses and accused the other of poison gas; Japanese forces are confirmed to have used it at least thirteen times.

The origin of the fighting is also contested. Several accounts say Ōyama opened fire at the airport gate. Harmsen holds the shootout was staged to cover a killing by Chinese soldiers disguised as guards, and Shi Shuo, of the 9th Group Army, said a death row inmate was dressed in uniform and killed. Whether Ōyama was acting on higher orders is unknown.
sections.legacy:
The battle was the first of twenty-two major engagements between the National Revolutionary Army and the Imperial Japanese Army, and is regarded by some historians as the first battle of the Second World War. It destroyed much of the city. The Chinese resistance shocked the Japanese, who believed they could take Shanghai within days and China within months. China failed to bring about international intervention, though Chiang kept troops in the city to influence the Nine-Power Treaty Conference then meeting in Brussels.

The Japanese advance on Nanjing began on 11 November, and the fighting led at once into the Battle of Nanjing. Japan did not immediately occupy the International Settlement or the French Concession, moving into them after declaring war on the United States and United Kingdom in 1941.

Harmsen wrote that it signalled the totality of modern urban warfare, and it was the largest urban battle before Stalingrad almost five years later. In 1940 the Chinese government named 14 August 1937 Air Force Day, after the 4th Flying Group under Gao Zhihang shot down six Japanese planes without loss. The defence of the Sihang Warehouse, watched by crowds across the creek, and the last stand at Baoshan became symbols of Chinese resistance.

summary: From 13 August to 26 November 1937 Chinese and Japanese forces fought for Shanghai on land, in the air and at sea. The Japanese took the city, but the Chinese held out for over three months and lost much of their best troops, and casualty figures remain widely disputed.
references: Benjamin Lai, Shanghai and Nanjing 1937: Massacre on the Yangtze (Osprey Publishing, 2017)
S. C. M. Paine, The Wars for Asia, 1911–1949 (Cambridge University Press, 2012)
Hans Van de Ven, China at War: Triumph and Tragedy in the Emergence of the New China, 1937–1952 (Profile Books, 2017)
Jay Taylor, The Generalissimo (Harvard University Press, 2009)
notes: The article's Order of battle section is empty, so strengths come only from the lead and the October and Luodian passages: around one million troops overall, over 200,000 Japanese against over 700,000 Chinese in early October.

Figures differ widely: China's official 187,200 killed and wounded vs 229,382 casualties vs 300,000 estimate; Japanese 9,115 killed and 31,257 injured vs Lai 93,000-99,000 vs Paulose 92,640. The article says the Ministry's Third War Zone total of 229,382 is exactly the same figure as the earlier battle-only count; I did not use that line to infer anything.
Black Saturday: the article gives 700-950 killed outright, 3,000 deaths and injuries, and separately 'an estimated 2,000 shoppers and passers-by' killed; I gave the first set only.
The article gives the Ōyama killing as Peace Preservation Corps guard plus two Japanese dead; accounts conflict (Ōyama armed or not), told in sources.

Article glitch: 'Japanese 6th Division left behind the Kunizaki Task Force' and several unit numbers read oddly; those details left out. Also the article's description of Battle of Jiashan is a single thin paragraph and was left out.

Left out for length: details of Liujiahang, Guangfu, Suzhou Creek unit by unit, the Songjiang fighting (Japanese claimed 5,286 captured, Hata suspects many were killed), and the Nine-Power Treaty Conference section, which is empty in the saved text.
